strengths: The dispatch problem is a clean, fully specified two-stage LP: stage 1 is the hourly net grid exchange g (gp, gm >= 0, dispatch.py:153), and stage 2 is per-scenario battery recourse plus imbalance (c, d, soc, up, dn, dispatch.py:154-155). Settlement re-solves stage 2 with g frozen (evaluate_commitment, dispatch.py:220-283). Because of this, every DFL loss can be defined exactly as realised settled cost, with no proxy needed.

Settlement is honest: the schedule is chosen without pv_actual, the terminal-SoC obligation is enforced in settlement as well as in commitment (policies.py:136-144), and an oracle defines regret (dispatch.py:286-292). This is exactly the regret definition DFL papers use, so results will be comparable with the literature.

The structure is convex: settled cost is a convex, piecewise-linear function of g for fixed realised PV, and HiGHS returns duals. A subgradient of realised cost with respect to the committed schedule is therefore available almost for free. That opens a cheap, exact route to decision-focused training that the exposé has not noticed yet.

The staged risk design in the exposé (Sec. 5, last paragraph, and Sec. 6) correctly names the zero-gradient problem of differentiating an LP and orders the work so that a thesis exists even if the layer fails.

The exposé frames a negative result as acceptable (Sec. 7, last paragraph). That is the right stance, because the analysis below suggests DFL headroom on this problem is narrow and confined to specific regimes.

The penalty-by-storage sensitivity grid (results/e2_sensitivity.csv) already exists. It is the right axis on which to look for DFL advantage, because storage coupling is the only place where pinball-at-the-right-quantile stops being decision-optimal.
notes:
The optimisation problem as implemented (dispatch.py), at S=40 and T=24: decision variables are the stage-1 net exchange g = gp - gm (24 values), plus stage-2 c, d, soc, up and dn for each scenario and hour. The forecast enters ONLY the right-hand side of the energy balance (load - pv). Storage couples the hours in stage 2, and that recourse is anticipative. The terminal-SoC constraint applies both in commitment and in settlement.

Here c is known and the feasible region of the recourse moves with PV, so the SPO+ surrogate and its Fisher-consistency result do not transfer. findings.title: Moving to real settled imbalance prices removes the asymmetric-penalty premise (German single-price reBAP) and makes the decision price-driven
findings.evidence: The exposé's motivation (Sec. 2, first paragraph) and its methodology (Sec. 5, 'Data'; Objective 3) assume asymmetric settlement: short at a punitive price, long for little. The CS1 tariff hard-codes this (configs/default.yaml:42-43; dispatch.py:196-197). German imbalance settlement (reBAP), and EU-harmonised imbalance pricing generally, is single-price: long and short deviations settle at the same price, though this should be verified for the zones and years used. Expected deviation cost is then roughly (reBAP - DA) times the deviation. That is linear in g, so the LP optimum becomes bang-bang or speculative, set by the sign of E[reBAP - DA | x], and it is unbounded without position limits. A further complication: the site PV is the national DE capacity factor rescaled to 2 MW (policies.py:58-60), so the site's forecast error IS the national solar forecast error. That error is a main driver of system imbalance and therefore of reBAP. Price and PV error are strongly dependent, and treating them independently is wrong. The exposé's weeks 3-4 (price acquisition) should already be finished by now (about week 6-7).
findings.recommendation: Before re-establishing baselines, decide the settlement model and write it down: (i) keep a stylised dual-price tariff (transparent, newsvendor structure intact, DFL question well-posed); (ii) use real single-price settlement with explicit position limits and a joint PV-price model (a harder problem, where the uncertain cost vector is price-driven); or (iii) report both. Do not mix real DA prices with a synthetic asymmetric imbalance penalty without saying so explicitly. If real reBAP is used, model its dependence on the national PV error. This dependence is the single most plausible source of a genuine DFL advantage, because a cost-trained model can learn to shade the forecast in exactly the hours where error and price co-move. A scoring-rule-trained marginal PV model cannot.

verification.reason: The exposé motivates the work with asymmetric settlement (Sec. 2). It also plans to replace the tariff with 'settled day-ahead and imbalance prices' (Sec. 3/5) and to headline results 'in euros on settled market prices' (Sec. 7). German reBAP is a single symmetric imbalance price, and EB GL harmonisation favours single pricing. So real settlement removes the asymmetric-newsvendor structure, and the commitment LP (gp >= 0 with no upper bound, dispatch.py:80-82) becomes price-speculative without position limits. The site PV is the national capacity factor times 2 MW (policies.py:58-60), so the site's error is the national solar error, which co-moves with system imbalance. The exposé's fallback (keep the synthetic tariff where data are missing) does not address this, because it assumes the problem is merely data availability. This is a design-level decision that must come first.

findings.title: Stage-2 recourse is anticipative: the battery sees the whole day's realised PV at hour 0
findings.evidence: evaluate_commitment solves one LP over all 24 hours with the full realised pv vector (dispatch.py:240-263). In solve_commitment, each scenario's recourse (c, d, soc, up, dn indexed by s,t; dispatch.py:154-155) likewise optimises with perfect knowledge of the scenario's whole path. Real intraday battery operation is non-anticipative, because it knows PV only up to t. This overstates the value of storage. That matters for DFL in particular: the analysis in finding 02 shows DFL can only beat a tau_t-quantile pipeline through storage coupling, which is exactly the part of the model this bias inflates (report.tex:793 attributes the storage effect to recourse).
findings.recommendation: Before DFL experiments, add a non-anticipative settlement option: a rolling-horizon re-solve, or at minimum a causal greedy battery rule that uses PV only up to t. Report the CS1 storage-grid result under both settlements. If the storage-driven gap shrinks, the DFL headroom shrinks with it, and that is better known in week 7 than in week 17. The training loss should use the same settlement as the evaluation.

verification.reason: evaluate_commitment builds a single 24-hour LP with the full realised pv vector and a frozen schedule (dispatch.py:240-263). The scenario recourse in solve_commitment is per-scenario and full-path as well. Battery settlement is therefore anticipative, and it inflates storage value, which report.tex:793 credits to recourse. Major is appropriate.

findings.title: The differentiable-layer plan underestimates problem size, the non-differentiable scenario generator, and the regularisation needed
findings.evidence: At S=40, T=24, one commitment LP has 2T + 5ST = 4,848 variables and 2ST = 1,920 equalities, plus 40 terminal and up to 41 CVaR rows (dispatch.py:153-186). A cvxpylayers/diffcp backward pass at this size per day, over roughly 700 training days per fold, across epochs, rolling folds, the 4x4 sensitivity grid, and several zones, is days of compute. OptNet/qpth uses dense KKT systems and does not scale to it. The LP solution is piecewise constant in pv, so the Jacobian dg/dpv is zero almost everywhere. A quadratic term (Wilder et al. 2019), a log-barrier/interior-point relaxation (Mandi & Guns 2020), or perturbed optimisers (Berthet et al. 2020) are required, and each changes the decision being learned. Upstream, scenarios_from_quantiles uses np.sort, np.interp at random uniforms, and clip (policies.py:49-55). Gradients through this are noisy, and the copula weight common_factor=0.75 is a fixed, untuned constant (policies.py:34). The exposé (Sec. 5) names the zero-gradient issue but none of these remedies, and it gives no compute budget.
findings.recommendation: If the layer arm is kept, scope it down. Use a deterministic-equivalent layer: one quantile path in, battery-aware schedule out, about 120 variables per day, with a small quadratic regulariser on g. Alternatively, use S of at most 8 fixed-quantile scenarios (no random sampling) so the map from quantiles to scenarios is a fixed linear map. Batch days with cvxpylayers and SCS, or use PyEPO. Benchmark one forward/backward pass in week 8 and extrapolate the full compute before committing weeks 14-17. Also note an alternative: the gradient of realised cost with respect to g is available exactly from the settlement LP duals, so the commitment layer only needs differentiating if the model outputs a forecast rather than a decision (see finding 06).

verification.reason: I verified the counts: 2T + 5ST = 48 + 4800 = 4848 variables and 2ST = 1920 equalities, plus 40 terminal and 41 CVaR rows. scenarios_from_quantiles uses sort, interp at random uniforms and clip, with fixed common_factor = 0.75 (policies.py:29-55). The exposé names no smoothing remedy and no compute budget (Sec. 5 only says 'differentiable convex optimisation layer'). It does acknowledge layer instability as a risk and sequences around it, which keeps this at major rather than higher.

findings.title: Missing arm: direct decision ERM with a linear model is a single convex LP and is the natural DFL method here (ridge was the best CS1 model)
findings.evidence: Ridge with about 55 features and residual-quantile intervals (models/baselines.py:85-133) has the best CRPS in CS1 (results/e1_leaderboard.csv: ridge raw CRPS 0.0304, ahead of gbm_quantile and lstm_quantile), and report.tex:573 cites ridge[cqr] as the cheapest model to act on. The features carry a mostly linear signal, the data are NWP-free, and there are only about 700 training days per fold. A high-capacity network trained on a 24-hour cost signal would be badly data-starved. Because settled cost is convex and piecewise linear in g for a given realised PV (finding 02), parameterising g_d,t = theta_h^T x_d,t (or pv_hat = theta^T x fed into a fixed deterministic dispatch) and minimising sum_d SettledCost(g_d; pv_d) + lambda*||theta||^2 is ONE convex LP/QP. It contains about 700 x 24 x 5 recourse variables (roughly 84k) and is solvable by HiGHS in seconds to minutes. This is the 'big-data newsvendor' / integrated ERM approach (Ban & Rudin 2019, Operations Research) extended with battery recourse. It finds the globally optimal decision-focused linear model, with no surrogate and no zero-gradient issue.
findings.recommendation: Make this the main DFL arm for weeks 10-13, replacing SPO+. Implement it by reusing _core_constraints with a decision rule in place of free g. It gives an exact upper reference: the best linear decision rule in hindsight on the training data. Any gradient-based layer method must approach it on the linear class, which makes it an internal validity check. Add features or a small nonlinear model only if ERM-linear clearly beats the tau_t-quantile baseline and residual analysis shows structure the linear model misses. Report model capacity explicitly as a factor: with ridge as the CS1 winner, expect DFL gains to come from re-targeting the bias and quantile level, not from representation.

verification.reason: Ridge has the best CRPS (raw 0.0302, cqr 0.0305; e1_leaderboard.csv) and the lowest regret, 144.3 (e2_by_model.csv). With battery recourse, settled cost for a fixed pv is an LP value function with g in the RHS, so it is convex in g. A linear decision rule therefore yields one convex LP, which makes the ERM argument sound. Caveats: this is a recommendation, not a defect. Its 'global optimum' inherits the anticipative-settlement bias from finding 04, and its scale (about 84k recourse variables, plus SoC constraints) should be benchmarked. Major as a missing strong arm is acceptable.

findings.title: The planned baselines are too weak: the 'strongest two-stage baseline' is not the stochastic program but a tuned, hour-specific quantile policy
findings.evidence: The exposé (Sec. 5, 'Baselines') proposes to retain the CS1 configurations 'unchanged': a conformalised quantile model, a point forecast, and the oracle. CS1's own numbers show these are not the strongest two-stage opponent. A single fixed q=0.55 gives regret 149.06 EUR/day (results/e2_quantile_sweep.csv; report.tex:545), against 159.82 for the stochastic program and 164.71 for point (results/e2_summary.csv). That figure was obtained by sweeping on the test days, so it is optimistic. Per finding 02, the optimal level differs by hour and regime (0.35 / 0.54 / 0.80), so a per-hour tau_t policy should do better still. The headroom is already small: stochastic beats point by only 3.0% (e2_summary.csv). A DFL model compared against point or stochastic would 'win' partly by finding the right quantile, which is a two-stage fix and not a DFL contribution.
findings.recommendation: Define the strongest two-stage baseline as follows. (1) Fit the CQR quantile model. (2) Apply ACI online recalibration (the CS1 result in e3_aci.csv). (3) Commit at analytically derived per-hour tau_t, or a tau_t vector tuned on a validation slice, never on test days. (4) Also run a stochastic program with tuned scenario dependence (common_factor) and tau_t-consistent marginals. Report DFL gains relative to the better of the two. The exposé's research question (Sec. 3) should be read as 'beyond the best tau_t-quantile pipeline'. Also re-run the e2 by-model table: ridge is missing from results/e2_by_model.csv even though report.tex:573 cites ridge regret values, so the numbers to beat need regenerating from one provenance.

verification.reason: The core claim holds. The sweep's q = 0.55 regret of 149.06 beats stochastic (159.82) and point (164.71) (e2_summary.csv), and stochastic beats point by only 2.97%. The sweep reuses the evaluation days (e2_dispatch.py:244, a subset of up to 120 days), so it is optimistic. The exposé retains the baselines 'unchanged' (Sec. 5). One sub-claim is false, however: ridge is NOT missing from results/e2_by_model.csv. Rows 18-19 contain ridge[cqr] at 144.32 and ridge[raw] at 144.82, matching report.tex:573. Drop the 'regenerate from one provenance' justification. Also note that the ridge regret of 144 is below the sweep's 149, so the stochastic summary row is not even the best existing number to beat.

findings.title: The 'cost-weighted quantile loss' is undefined, and the conditions under which DFL can win are not stated
findings.evidence: Sec. 5 calls it 'a cost-weighted quantile loss, which needs no differentiable solver' and gives no formula. Given finding 02, the natural definition is pinball at tau_t with weight (penalty_up + penalty_down), plus a kink term at g=0. That is exact DFL at battery 0, so this arm and 'DFL' coincide there. DFL can strictly beat it only through: (i) intertemporal battery coupling, under which per-hour quantiles stop being optimal because the battery shifts which hour's error matters; (ii) the import/export kink; (iii) day-varying or uncertain prices, under which tau becomes stochastic and correlated with the error (finding 03); (iv) a terminal-SoC obligation; (v) misspecification of the quantile model. With anticipative recourse (finding 04), the size of (i) is inflated. results/e2_sensitivity.csv shows the stochastic-vs-point advantage is non-monotone and strongly regime-dependent (2.7% to 67%).
findings.recommendation: Write the loss explicitly in the methods chapter and prove or state the battery=0 equivalence. Then frame the hypotheses as: DFL advantage is about 0 at battery=0 under a fixed tariff, and grows with storage size and price variability and with price-error correlation. Test these hypotheses on the existing penalty-by-storage grid, extended with a price-variability axis. This turns a possibly null result into a clean, predicted, mechanism-level finding.

verification.reason: The exposé names the 'cost-weighted quantile loss' with no formula (Sec. 3/5) and states no conditions under which DFL can win. e2_sensitivity.csv indeed ranges from 2.7% (600/0) to 67.5% (150/2) and is non-monotone. The mechanism list is sound, subject to the same caveat as finding 02: at battery = 0 the equivalence is pinball within each import or export regime, plus the kink at g = 0.

findings.title: Risk-averse (CVaR) and calibration interactions with DFL are not scoped
findings.evidence: solve_commitment supports a CVaR blend (dispatch.py:141-200), and CS1 found both risk-averse policies cost more in total (results/e2_summary.csv: cvar regret 198.4, quantile 207.7, point 164.7). Sub-question 3 plans conformal calibration on top of decision-trained models. For a model trained to output a decision quantile tau_t directly, 'calibration' must be defined at that single level per hour. Full-interval coverage is not even defined for an ERM decision rule that outputs g.
findings.recommendation: Train DFL against the risk-neutral expected-cost objective only. Leave CVaR as a footnote, since CS1 shows it is cost-dominated under this tariff. For the calibration audit, define coverage at the decision level (empirical P(pv <= committed quantile) against tau_t, by hour and by month). Apply ACI to that single level instead of to 90% intervals.

verification.reason: The numbers check out against e2_summary.csv: cvar regret 198.4, quantile 207.7 and point 164.7, so both risk-averse policies cost more. Sub-question 3 (calibration on top of decision-trained models) is underspecified for a model that outputs a decision. This is a reasonable scoping note, and minor is the right severity.

strengths: All 12 references in exposé section 8 exist, and the authors, year and venue are essentially correct. I spot-checked each one. Elmachtoub & Grigas, Mgmt Sci 68(1):9-26, doi 10.1287/mnsc.2020.3922: correct. Gneiting & Katzfuss, ARSIA 1:125-151: correct. Hong et al., IJF 32(3):896-913: correct. Pinson, Chevallier & Kariniotakis, IEEE TPWRS 22(3):1148-1156: correct. Morales et al. 2014, Springer, doi 10.1007/978-1-4614-9411-9: correct. Mandi et al., JAIR vol. 80, pp. 1623-1701, doi 10.1613/jair.1.15320: matches DBLP; arXiv's journal-ref says vol. 81, which is the outlier. Agrawal 2019 (NeurIPS 32), Amos & Kolter 2017 (ICML), Donti 2017 (NeurIPS 30), Romano 2019 (NeurIPS 32) and Gibbs & Candès 2021 (NeurIPS 34): all correct. The only bibliographic error is in Yu et al. (2024); see the minor finding.

The core lineage is cited correctly and is the right one: newsvendor-style quantile bidding (Pinson 2007), stochastic programming for renewables (Morales 2014), scoring rules (Gneiting & Katzfuss, GEFCom2014), conformal methods (CQR, ACI), and DFL foundations (SPO+, OptNet, cvxpylayers, Donti task-based learning, the Mandi survey). Few master's exposés have a reference spine this clean.

The research questions on what is sacrificed (calibration and coverage of decision-trained models), on drift, and on cross-zone portability are in fact under-studied in the value-oriented renewable forecasting literature I found. Most papers (Carriere 2019, Stratigakos 2022, Zhang 2024, Wahdany 2023) report cost only, on one site and a fixed split. This is where the thesis's real novelty can be placed.

The exposé already anticipates the hardest technical risk, the zero gradient almost everywhere when differentiating through an LP (§5), and it states an honest negative outcome (§7). Both match what the DFL literature warns about.

The plan to replace the synthetic tariff with settled day-ahead and imbalance prices addresses the most common weakness of DFL energy papers: synthetic or IEEE-bus test cases (Zhang et al. 2022 use IEEE 30-bus; Yu et al. 2024 use IEEE test systems).
notes:
I checked all 12 references in exposé §8 against web sources. The only bibliographic error is in Yu et al. 2024. I have medium-high confidence in the NeurIPS/ICML entries, which match my knowledge and are standard; the journal entries were confirmed by search. I could not confirm the venue of Sang et al. (journal version vs arXiv:2305.00362), so check it on IEEE Xplore before citing.

The most urgent points:
- **Gap statement:** it overclaims and must be reworded. Suggested wording is in literature-gap-claim-overstated.
- **SPO+:** it does not fit the inherited LP, because the forecast is on the RHS (src/riskaware_pv/decision/dispatch.py:101-103). This should be decided before the planned weeks 10-13.
- **Newsvendor equivalence:** at zero storage, the 'cost-weighted quantile loss' is already the exact decision loss, so DFL gains can only come from storage coupling and time-varying price ratios.

The defensible novelty is the combination of a calibration/coverage audit of decision-trained models, conformal recalibration on top, robustness to drift and retraining, and cross-zone transfer under real settlement rules, all run under a leakage-audited rolling-origin protocol. The prior trading-DFL papers I found largely do not report these.

findings.evidence:

findings.recommendation: Rewrite §4 and the gap paragraph now, before more implementation is done. The original weeks 1-2 literature phase has already passed. Add a 'Value-oriented forecasting for renewable trading' paragraph built on (1)-(9), and cite the Li et al. review as the field overview. Replace the gap statement with something defensible, for example: 'Value-oriented and decision-focused forecasting for renewable trading has been demonstrated, mostly for single sites, a single market, fixed train/test splits, and with cost as the only reported metric (Carriere & Kariniotakis, 2019; Muñoz et al., 2020; Stratigakos et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). It remains open how (a) different DFL formulations compare against a strong, calibrated two-stage baseline under the same leakage-audited rolling-origin protocol, (b) what decision-focused training costs in calibration and interval validity, and whether conformal recalibration recovers it, (c) whether the advantage persists under drift and retraining, and (d) whether it transfers across bidding zones with different settlement rules.' Neither claim holds against the existing work. findings.title: SPO+ assumes the predicted quantity sits in a linear objective, but here the PV forecast enters the right-hand side of the balance constraints
findings.evidence: Exposé §3 (line 309, line 318), §4 (line 336), §5 (line 350) and §6 (weeks 10-13, line 370) make SPO+ one of the three core arms. Elmachtoub & Grigas (2022) define SPO/SPO+ for min_w c^T w with c predicted and the feasible set fixed. In the repo, the forecast enters the constraints, not the cost. In src/riskaware_pv/decision/dispatch.py:101-103 the energy balance is 'b = load[t] - pv[s, t]', i.e. b_eq (RHS). The cost vector c (dispatch.py:196-197, 260-261) holds only the tariff and penalties. With uncertain RHS the feasible region moves with the forecast, so the SPO+ surrogate and its Fisher-consistency guarantee do not apply directly. PyEPO (Tang & Khalil, 2024) likewise supports only predicted objective coefficients. Zhang et al. (arXiv:2405.09004) state this limitation explicitly: pinball and SPO-type losses target single-stage problems and do not handle redispatch.
findings.recommendation: Decide this before week 10. Option A: reformulate. Under a fixed recourse policy the stage-2 cost can be written as a function of the forecast, and you can use the analytical piecewise-linear value-oriented loss of Zhang et al. (2024/2025), which is built for exactly this DA+RT structure with an LP recourse. Option B: replace the SPO+ arm with a method that handles RHS/constraint uncertainty. Candidates are Donti et al. (2017) task-based learning through the stochastic program; cvxpylayers with a small quadratic regulariser (Wilder, Dilkina & Tambe, 2019, AAAI 33, 1658-1665); the interior-point/log-barrier relaxation (Mandi & Guns, 2020, NeurIPS 33); perturbed optimisers (Berthet et al., 2020, NeurIPS 33); and locally learned decision losses (Shah et al., 2022, NeurIPS 35). If SPO+ stays in the plan, the thesis must explicitly derive the reformulation that puts the uncertainty into the objective and state that the consistency result no longer applies.

verification.reason: The technical claim is confirmed. In dispatch.py:101-103 the PV forecast enters the equality right-hand side (b = load[t] - pv[s,t]), and the cost vector at dispatch.py:196-201 holds only tariffs and penalties, so no forecast-dependent objective coefficient exists for SPO+ to target. SPO+ as defined by Elmachtoub & Grigas (min c^T w with predicted c and a fixed feasible set) therefore does not apply directly. Its consistency guarantee does not carry over either, and the exposé's §5 statement that SPO+ 'has consistency guarantees for linear objectives' is misapplied here. I adjusted the severity from critical to major. It affects one of three arms (weeks 10-13), the exposé's staged design keeps a reportable thesis without it, and the fix is a design decision (reformulate, or swap in a method that handles RHS uncertainty) due before week 10. It is not a threat to the thesis as a whole.

findings.title: Without storage, the 'cheap cost-weighted quantile loss' already is the exact decision-focused loss, which the literature has known since Pinson 2007, Gneiting 2011, and Ban & Rudin 2019
findings.evidence: The docstring in dispatch.py:14-19 states the newsvendor result itself. With linear asymmetric penalties (configs/default.yaml:42-43, 300 vs 90 EUR/MWh), the realised-cost-minimising commitment is the tau = 300/390 ≈ 0.77 quantile. The empirical risk under cost is then exactly a pinball loss at that tau. See Gneiting, T. (2011), Quantiles as optimal point forecasts, IJF 27(2), 197-207; Ban, G.-Y., & Rudin, C. (2019), The big data newsvendor, Operations Research 67(1), 90-108; Muñoz et al. (2020). The exposé (§3 line 318, §5 line 350) presents the cost-weighted quantile loss as just a 'cheap baseline' and contrasts it with 'training it on a proper scoring rule'. A scoring-rule model read off at the critical quantile is already close to decision-optimal in the zero-storage corner of the grid.
findings.recommendation: State the equivalence in the thesis. Then frame the DFL contribution as coming only from what the newsvendor does not capture: (i) intertemporal coupling through the battery (the storage axis of the grid), (ii) time-varying, price-dependent critical ratios once real imbalance prices are used, and (iii) scenario-based commitment against the full distribution. Expect and pre-register near-zero DFL gains at storage = 0, and use that as a sanity check. Add Bertsimas, D., & Kallus, N. (2020), From predictive to prescriptive analytics, Management Science 66(3), 1025-1044, and Sadana, U., et al. (2025), A survey of contextual optimization methods for decision-making under uncertainty, EJOR 320(2), 271-289. Both are framing references for the 'estimate-then-optimise vs integrated' taxonomy.

verification.reason: The general point is valid: with zero storage and linear penalties, the cost-optimal commitment is a quantile and empirical cost reduces to a pinball-type loss. The specific evidence is wrong, however. The critical ratio is not 300/390 ≈ 0.77, because the commitment also carries the day-ahead price. The repo already handles this: policies.py:158-169 computes cu = penalty_up - import_price_offpeak, giving (300-120)/390 ≈ 0.46. In reality it varies by hour (peak 220 gives ≈0.21) and by sign (export at 45 gives a different ratio), with a kink at g = 0, and the forecast target is PV, so the relevant quantile is of load minus PV. The exposé is also already aware of the newsvendor result: §2 cites Pinson 2007 for the quantile bid, §7 names 'choosing the commitment quantile well' as the likely negative-result explanation, and Case Study 1 already showed the storage complementarity (e2_dispatch.py:129-142). The useful residue is to state the equivalence explicitly and to pre-register near-zero DFL gains over the cost-weighted quantile at storage = 0. findings.title: With real prices, the dual-price 'punitive short / cheap long' story may not match the target markets. German reBAP and Nordic settlement are single-price
findings.evidence: Exposé §2 (opening paragraph) bases the problem on asymmetric dual-price settlement (Pinson 2007, whose setting is dual-price). Objective 3 (§3) and §5 'Data' plan to switch to settled day-ahead and imbalance prices across several zones. Germany's reBAP is a single imbalance price whose sign and level depend on the system imbalance, and the Nordic area moved to single pricing in 2021. Under single pricing the imbalance price is itself uncertain at gate closure. The optimal bid then depends on a joint forecast of generation and imbalance price (Zugno, Jónsson & Pinson, 2013, Trading wind energy on the basis of probabilistic forecasts both of wind generation and of market quantities, Wind Energy 16(6), 909-926; Stratigakos et al., 2021, value-oriented price forecasting). None of this literature is cited.
findings.recommendation: Add a short subsection on imbalance settlement design, and decide early (weeks 3-4 work is due now) which zones and settlement regimes are in scope. Also decide whether imbalance prices are treated as known ex post (realised cost only) or forecast ex ante (which would make it a joint forecasting problem). Cite Zugno et al. (2013) and Stratigakos et al. (2021) for the price-uncertainty side, and state the per-zone settlement rule in the data section. Without this, euro 'regret on real prices' figures are not comparable across zones, and the portability question (sub-question 5) gets confounded by market design.

With real prices the penalty asymmetry is therefore stochastic and sign-dependent rather than a fixed 300/90 ratio, and the commitment problem becomes partly a price-forecasting problem (Zugno et al. 2013). The exposé and report.tex cite none of this, and the weeks 3-4 data deliverable depends on the choice. Major is appropriate.

findings.title: Most real imbalance regimes use a single price, so the exposé's asymmetric 'short is punitive, long is cheap' framing does not hold for them
findings.evidence: Exposé §2 says short positions are bought back at a punitive rate while long positions are absorbed for little, and the case study uses fixed asymmetric penalties of 300 and 90 EUR/MWh (configs/default.yaml:42-43; report.tex:323). Real settlement differs. DE reBAP is one symmetric quarter-hour price that can be positive or negative (netztransparenz). GB has used a single cash-out price since P305 went live on 5 Nov 2015 (Elexon). The Nordic TSOs, including Energinet DK1/DK2, moved to single price, single position on 1 Nov 2021 (Fingrid/eSett); before that they used dual production prices. Under a single price the cost of a deviation is (lambda_imb - lambda_DA) x deviation. Its sign and size are random, time-varying and correlated with the system-wide forecast error. The optimal quantile is therefore not a fixed penalty ratio, and it may sit close to the median. The 'penalty-by-storage grid' (Objective 4) then has no real-market counterpart for these zones, and the value of decision-focused learning could shrink a lot. That outcome would be a valid result, but the design has to expect it.
findings.recommendation: Decide now and write down how cost is defined: realised cost = DA revenue + (actual - committed) x lambda_imb per settlement period, using settled prices. Keep the synthetic asymmetric grid as a separate, clearly labelled stylised experiment. Report the empirical distribution of (lambda_imb - lambda_DA) and of its sign-conditional means per zone and year before training anything. That is the real 'penalty ratio', and it tells you early whether decision-focused learning has room to win.

However, this does not threaten the thesis's validity or feasibility. Decision-focused learning stays well defined under a stochastic, error-correlated spread, and the stylised penalty grid remains a legitimate controlled experiment. It is a framing and cost-definition decision that must be made early, which makes it major rather than critical. The recommendation (define realised cost as DA revenue + deviation x lambda_imb, and inspect the spread distribution first) is sound.

findings.title: A national aggregate rescaled to one site, settled against a national imbalance price, builds in an error-price correlation no single BRP faces
findings.evidence: The target is the German national solar aggregate scaled by its 99.9th percentile (opsd.py:215-222) and then multiplied by pv_nameplate_mw (policies.py:60). reBAP and the GB system price are driven by the system imbalance, and in a solar-heavy system the national solar forecast error is a large part of that imbalance. Settling a scaled copy of the national error at reBAP therefore gives the 'site' the full system correlation, which raises or lowers costs systematically. A real 2 MW plant's error is only partly correlated with the national error. A BRP holding the whole national fleet would also not be a price-taker.

Then state explicitly that the error-price correlation is realistic for a portfolio and overstated for a single site. (b) Add de-correlated site series, for example TSO control-area solar (50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW on ENTSO-E and netztransparenz) or an open single-site PV dataset, as a sensitivity check. In either case, report results both with real lambda_imb and with lambda_imb shuffled within its month and hour, to separate forecast value from correlation effects.

findings.title: Primary metric (regret vs oracle) is undefined once storage and real settled prices are combined
findings.evidence: CS1 regret is defined against synthetic, known, asymmetric penalties: config default.yaml market (300/90 EUR/MWh, a TOU import tariff) and the oracle in dispatch.py:286-292. Exposé Obj 3 / §5 Data replaces these with settled day-ahead and imbalance prices, which raises four problems. (a) German imbalance settlement (reBAP) is single-price: the long/short asymmetry is not a parameter but arises from the correlation between the price and the system state, and the price is unknown at gate closure. (b) An oracle that knows the realised imbalance price and PV can arbitrage the imbalance market with the battery, so regret would mostly measure price foresight rather than PV forecast quality. (c) The target is national aggregate PV scaled to a 2 MW site (report.tex:832-834). Its forecast error is therefore highly correlated with the German system imbalance and the reBAP sign, an artefact no real single site has, and it will distort decision value in an unknown direction. (d) The 'penalty-by-storage grid' (§5 Evaluation) cannot be swept with real prices, because penalty is no longer a free parameter. In addition, the exposé §2 describes a renewable generator trading, while the actual LP is a prosumer with load, TOU imports and feed-in exports (dispatch.py:1-20).
findings.recommendation: Define the metric formally in a one-page evaluation protocol. Regret_d = cost(policy_d) - cost(PV-oracle_d), where the oracle knows realised PV but faces the same price information set as the policy (day-ahead prices known, imbalance price as expected or forecast at the gate), and both are settled ex post on realised prices. Report absolute cost and regret, plus the percentage of the gap closed with a CI. Keep two evaluation regimes, stated explicitly. Regime A, mechanism: the synthetic asymmetric tariff, with the penalty × storage grid. Regime B, external validity: one DE case using real day-ahead and reBAP prices (2018-2020) as a single robustness check, with the national-aggregate correlation caveat stated. Align the §2 framing with the prosumer LP actually being solved, or change the LP.

verification.reason: The substance checks out. CS1 regret uses the synthetic tariff (configs/default.yaml market: 300/90 penalties, TOU 220/120, export 45) and a perfect-PV oracle (dispatch.py:286-292). PV enters the RHS b = load - pv (dispatch.py:104). The LP is a prosumer with load, TOU imports and feed-in exports (dispatch.py:1-20, report.tex:319-321), not the 'renewable generator trading' of exposé §2. German reBAP is single-price, so penalty asymmetry is not a free parameter, and the grid in §5 cannot be swept on real prices. The national-aggregate target (report.tex:832-834) correlating with system imbalance is a legitimate confound. Point (b), oracle imbalance arbitrage, is plausible but depends on implementation choices that don't exist yet. It is not critical, because the exposé (§5, last paragraph) already has a fallback ('the synthetic tariff is retained ... and the limitation is reported'), so Regime A stays viable. It is a decision to make early, so major.

findings.title: CS1's effect sizes sit at the noise floor; the thesis needs paired tests, all test days and multiple seeds or its comparisons will be uninterpretable
findings.evidence: I recomputed these from results/e2_daily.csv. The headline stochastic-vs-point gain is 4.89 EUR/day (SD of paired differences 30.9, n=200, t≈2.24). The 200-day subsample (report.tex:514) gives a minimum detectable effect of about 6.1 EUR/day (3.7% of regret) at 80% power. The exposé's motivating 'inversions' (§2) are 161.74 vs 162.13 and 144.32 vs 144.82 EUR/day (results/e2_by_model.csv), differences of 0.4-0.5 EUR, roughly 10× below what is detectable. CS1 says explicitly that it ran no significance tests (report.tex:752), used three folds (report.tex:840) and one seed (report.tex:862). DFL training through a differentiable LP is non-convex and seed-sensitive, so the variation between seeds could exceed the effect.
findings.recommendation: (1) Settle every test day (about 700+ days over 2018-2020, at 0.16 s per LP), not a 200-day subsample. (2) Make the delivery day the unit of inference. Test the paired daily cost differences with a Diebold-Mariano test using HAC (Newey-West) variance, and give 95% CIs from a moving-block bootstrap (block of about 7 days). (3) Train every stochastic model on at least 5 seeds, average over seeds before the paired test, and report the spread between seeds separately. (4) Pre-register a small set of primary comparisons, apply a Holm correction, and use a Model Confidence Set when ranking many configurations. (5) Run a power calculation now from the e2_daily.csv SD and state the minimum detectable effect in the methods chapter. (6) Drop the 'pairs invert' claim from the motivation, or restate it as 'not statistically distinguishable'.

findings.title: The planned comparison is confounded by model class, decision rule, tuning effort, and a commitment quantile chosen on test data
findings.evidence: (a) CS1's best models are ridge and GBM (e2_by_model.csv). Gradient DFL (cvxpylayers/SPO+) needs a differentiable model such as a linear model or MLP, so a 'DFL vs best baseline' comparison mixes loss with model class. (b) The baselines use stochastic SAA over 40 common-factor scenarios (report.tex:317-327), whereas a DFL point forecast is normally plugged into a deterministic LP. That confounds the loss with the decision rule and with the scenario generator. (c) Exposé §5 Baselines keeps the baselines 'retained unchanged', and CS1 did no hyperparameter search (report.tex:752), while DFL gets 4-week tuning phases (§6 wks 10-17). That tuning asymmetry favours DFL. (d) The CS1 q=0.55 optimum (report.tex:545) was selected on the same days it is scored on (experiments/e2_dispatch.py:92-121 uses the test-day frames). (e) With no storage the problem is a newsvendor, so pinball loss at the critical fractile is already decision-optimal. The 'cost-weighted quantile loss' is therefore the correct two-stage optimum, not a DFL variant, and any DFL gain can only come from intertemporal coupling through the battery.
findings.recommendation: Use a factorial comparison within one model class: loss {pinball/CRPS, cost-weighted critical-fractile pinball, DFL} × model {linear, small MLP} × decision rule {deterministic plug-in, tuned-quantile plug-in, SAA}, all with identical features and folds. Give baselines and DFL the same tuning budget on the same validation split. Choose the commitment quantile and every hyperparameter on validation days, never on test days. Report CS1's ridge+SAA and tuned-quantile ridge as external reference rows, but test hypotheses only within a model class.

(c) Exposé §5 says the baselines are 'retained unchanged', CS1 did no hyperparameter search (report.tex:752), and DFL gets multi-week tuning phases (§6). findings.title: SPO+ does not directly apply: the uncertain quantity (PV) is in the constraints, not the linear cost vector
findings.evidence: Exposé §3 Obj 2 and §4 invoke SPO+ and its 'consistency guarantees for linear objectives' (Elmachtoub & Grigas 2022). SPO+ assumes min c^T x over a known feasible set with c predicted. In dispatch.py:96-125 PV enters the right-hand side of the energy-balance equality (b = load - pv), and the cost coefficients (prices and penalties) are known. The guarantees therefore do not transfer, and a naive SPO+ implementation would not be well-posed. This threatens SQ2 ('which formulation performs best') as written.
findings.recommendation: Replace SPO+ in the core plan with a method that handles uncertainty in the constraints or in the recourse. Options include task-based end-to-end learning through the two-stage problem (Donti et al. 2017, already cited), a quadratically regularised LP layer (cvxpylayers), or perturbed-optimiser gradients. Keep SPO+ only if you derive a valid reformulation, for example a recourse-cost representation, and state the assumptions explicitly. Reword SQ2 as 'cheap cost-weighted loss vs one full differentiable-optimisation method'.

verification.reason: SPO+ (Elmachtoub & Grigas 2022) assumes min c^T x over a known feasible set, with c being the predicted quantity. In dispatch.py:96-110 the uncertain PV enters the equality RHS (b = load[t] - pv[s,t]), and the prices and penalties in c are known config constants. SPO+ and its consistency guarantees do not apply as stated in exposé §3 Obj 2 and §4/§5. A side note that helps the student: because PV sits in the RHS, the LP optimal value is piecewise linear (not piecewise constant) in the prediction. The §5 risk statement ('true gradient is zero almost everywhere') describes cost-vector uncertainty, which is the wrong case here, and makes a differentiable-layer or Donti-style approach more tractable than the exposé fears. Major is appropriate.

strengths: Test suite is green and fast: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q` gives 22 passed in 9.5 s (Python 3.11.15, torch 2.14.0, scipy 1.17.1). You can run it on every commit while developing the thesis code.

The feature layer is leakage-safe by construction. Every autoregressive feature goes through `_gated_shift`, which asserts at runtime that no lag post-dates the origin (src/riskaware_pv/data/features.py:53-58). On top of that, tests/test_no_leakage.py:35-67 poisons the series after the gate and checks the design matrix does not change, and it does this for gates 6, 12 and 18. This is the audited base the exposé (Section 5) promises.

There is one model interface (`Forecaster`: fit/predict/predict_quantiles, models/base.py:32-104) and a factory registry (pipeline.py:78-113). Every fold gets a fresh model, so a decision-focused model can be added as one more registry entry and is scored through the same backtest, conformal wrapper (`ConformalizedQuantile`) and dispatch policies as the baselines.

The LSTM is already in PyTorch, with a monotone quantile head that cannot produce crossing quantiles (models/neural.py:67-92), a hand-written training loop (neural.py:217-233) and gradient clipping. Swapping its loss for a decision loss changes only a few lines; no framework migration is needed.

The dispatch LP is a clean, fully linear two-stage program: energy balance, SoC dynamics, an optional CVaR term via Rockafellar-Uryasev, and a terminal SoC constraint (decision/dispatch.py:93-217). The `_Vars` block allocator makes the variable layout explicit, so it can be ported one-to-one to cvxpy. It is also fast. I measured 1.6 ms per solve with one scenario and 64 ms with 40 scenarios, so SPO+-style training with one LP solve per day and epoch is affordable (about 730 days x 25 epochs x 2 ms, roughly 40 s per fold).

Settlement is kept separate from commitment: `evaluate_commitment` fixes the stage-1 schedule and settles it against realised PV (dispatch.py:220-283). That is exactly the realised-cost / regret oracle a decision-focused training loss and its evaluation both need. Property tests check that the oracle is a lower bound, that a perfect forecast attains oracle cost, and the energy balance (tests/test_dispatch.py).

findings.title: PV uncertainty enters the dispatch LP in the constraint right-hand side, not the cost vector, so SPO+ cannot be applied as the exposé describes
findings.evidence: In dispatch.py:100-110 forecast PV appears only in b_eq (`b = load[t] - pv[s, t]`). The cost vector c (dispatch.py:190-200) holds only prices and penalties. SPO+ (Elmachtoub & Grigas 2022, exposé Sections 3 and 5) is defined for linear objectives whose *cost coefficients* are predicted. With the predicted quantity in the RHS, the SPO+ surrogate and its consistency guarantee do not carry over. The Week 10-13 phase in the exposé (Section 6) assumes they do.
findings.recommendation: Decide now, before Week 7-9 work starts, how SPO+ maps onto this problem. Options: (a) reformulate so PV appears in the objective, e.g. eliminate the recourse and write the imbalance cost as a piecewise-linear function of the forecast (newsvendor form), which is valid without a battery or with a fixed battery policy; (b) replace SPO+ with a method designed for RHS/constraint uncertainty (e.g. the differentiable layer, or a direct regret-gradient approach such as perturbed optimizers); (c) keep SPO+ only for a price-forecasting variant. Write the chosen mathematical formulation into the thesis methodology before implementing anything.

verification.reason: The technical claim holds. In dispatch.py:100-104 forecast PV enters only b_eq (`b = load[t] - pv[s, t]`), and c (dispatch.py:190-198) holds only prices and penalties. SPO+ as defined by Elmachtoub & Grigas assumes predicted linear cost coefficients, and the exposé itself restates this ('consistency guarantees for linear objectives'), so the Week 10-13 SPO+ arm has no valid formulation yet. Downgraded from critical to major: this is one of three staged arms, the exposé deliberately keeps cheaper fallbacks (the cost-weighted loss in Weeks 7-9 and the differentiable layer), and the thesis stays feasible. It is still a methodology decision to settle before Week 10, not a validity threat to the whole thesis.

findings.title: Real day-ahead and imbalance prices make the commitment LP unbounded and silently drop days from the results
findings.evidence: I verified this by running the LP. Setting export_price=250 > import gives 'The problem is unbounded' (HiGHS status 10). A negative off-peak import price (-50) also gives unbounded. The causes: gp/gm have no upper bound (dispatch.py:80-82), import and export are not mutually exclusive, there is no grid-connection limit, and charge/discharge can run simultaneously. Real DE day-ahead prices go negative and use one price for buying and selling. The German imbalance price (reBAP) is single-price and can be negative, so the fixed up/down penalty structure (config.py:91-92) does not describe the real market. When a solve fails, run_policy returns total_cost=NaN (policies.py:133-134). summarise_policies then takes the mean, which skips NaNs, while `n_days` (e2_dispatch.py:85) still counts those rows, so failed days disappear from the cost averages without notice.
findings.recommendation: Before switching to real prices: add grid import/export limits (P_grid_max) as bounds on gp, gm, up and dn. Accept time-varying price vectors (`price_da[t]`, `price_imb_up[t]`, `price_imb_dn[t]`) instead of MarketConfig scalars. Add a test with negative and single-price inputs that asserts status=='optimal'. Make run_policy raise on unbounded or infeasible instead of returning NaN, or at least count and report dropped days. Also decide explicitly how a single-price imbalance market (reBAP) changes the asymmetric-penalty story in the thesis. Under symmetric settlement the newsvendor argument, and much of the expected decision-focused gain, may vanish.

verification.reason: Reproduced with the repo code (PYTHONPATH=src .venv python). With default config the solve is optimal. export_price=250 gives 'The problem is unbounded (HiGHS Status 10)', and so does import_price_offpeak=-50. gp/gm are bounded only below (dispatch.py:80-82). This is not hypothetical: the cached DE panel (data/interim/opsd_de_panel.parquet) already holds price_eur_mwh from 2018-09-30 to 2020-09-30 with 484 negative hours. A failed solve returns total_cost=NaN (policies.py:133-134), summarise_policies uses mean(), which skips NaN, while n_days uses g.size() (e2_dispatch.py:85), so failed days vanish silently. CS1 itself is unaffected: all 1000 rows in e2_daily.csv are 'optimal'. The code fix is easy. Critical is kept because the single-price reBAP point undercuts the exposé's core premise ('asymmetric prices... a punitive rate', Section 2), and the constant-penalty structure (config.py:90-92) does not survive contact with real settlement.

findings.title: With real prices the commitment would use the realised day-ahead price at gate closure, which is look-ahead the leakage guard does not check
findings.evidence: Today the stage-1 LP reads a synthetic tariff that is known in advance (`import_price_vector`, dispatch.py:70-73). The exposé (Section 3, objective 3) replaces it with settled day-ahead prices. Those clear after gate closure, so feeding realised D+1 prices into `solve_commitment` at decision time is look-ahead. tests/test_no_leakage.py only checks `build_design_matrix` and the LSTM sequences. Nothing tests the decision inputs (prices, load) or the decision-focused training path, which the exposé (Section 5) promises to cover.
findings.recommendation: Separate decision-time price information (a price forecast, or prices known at the gate) from settlement prices (realised, used only in evaluate_commitment and in the training loss). Add a decision-layer leakage test: poison post-gate prices and imbalance prices and assert the committed schedules are unchanged. Training losses may use realised prices because they are labels, but inference must not.

verification.reason: Correct as a design hazard. The stage-1 LP reads `import_price_vector` (dispatch.py:70-73, 188), and the leakage tests cover only build_design_matrix and the LSTM encoder (tests/test_no_leakage.py:35-143). No test touches decision inputs. However, this is a future pitfall in code not yet written, not an existing leak. Many price-taker studies also treat day-ahead prices as known or replace them with a forecast as an explicit, documented assumption. Major (decide and document early, add the poisoning test), not critical.

findings.title: The model interface has no way to pass decision context, and the backtest swallows TypeError
findings.evidence: `Forecaster.fit(X, y)` (base.py:93-94) receives no prices, load, battery or market parameters, and no day grouping. A decision-focused model needs all of these to compute its loss. The backtest calls `model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, history=history)` and falls back to `fit(X_tr, y_tr)` on *any* TypeError (backtest.py:84-91). A genuine TypeError raised inside a new decision-focused fit would be silently retried without its context and still produce numbers. The backtest also passes `history=X`, the full frame including the test fold (backtest.py:126; drift/policies.py:43). The LSTM only reads windows ending at the origin, but a new model that touches `history` freely would leak.
findings.recommendation: Extend the contract explicitly: `fit(X, y, *, history=None, decision_ctx=None)` on the base class, with a `DecisionContext` dataclass holding per-day price, load, battery and market data. Delete the try/except TypeError. Pass a gated history accessor, or a frame truncated at the fold's train end, instead of the full X.

verification.reason: Verified. The abstract `fit(self, X, y)` takes no decision context (base.py:~93). `_fit` catches any TypeError and silently retries without history (backtest.py:84-91), and the same pattern appears in drift/policies.py:~40-46. `_fit(factory, fit_on, history=X)` passes the full frame including test folds (backtest.py:126). Severity is appropriate.

findings.title: LSTM training samples random rows rather than whole days, and the post-processing is outside the computation graph
findings.evidence: neural.py:221-228 builds minibatches from `torch.randperm(n)` over hourly rows, and in k-space night rows are dropped (base.py:81-90). The conversion from k to MW (base.py:64-70), the clipping and the night clamp (base.py:72-79), and the national-to-site scaling (`_as_site_mw`, policies.py:58-60) are all done in numpy after prediction, so no gradient can flow through them.

Re-implement the target-space inverse, the night mask and the nameplate scaling as differentiable torch ops so the decision layer receives forecasts in MW. findings.title: Delivery days and the gate are defined in UTC, but the EPEX day-ahead gate is 12:00 CET/CEST
findings.evidence: configs/default.yaml:13 sets `gate_hour: 12 # (UTC)`. forecast_origin (features.py:29-35) normalises days in UTC. findings.title: Policy comparisons share one RNG stream, so adding a policy or model shifts the baseline numbers
findings.evidence: In e2_dispatch.py:52-64 a single `rng` is consumed sequentially by 'stochastic' and 'cvar' on every day, so the two policies see different scenario sets (no common random numbers). Inserting a new decision-focused policy, or changing the policy order, changes every later scenario draw. The 'baselines retained unchanged' that the exposé promises (Section 5, Baselines) would then quietly move.
findings.recommendation: Derive the scenario RNG per (date, model) with `np.random.default_rng([seed, date_ordinal])`, generate scenarios once per day, and share them across all scenario-based policies. Freeze the CS1 baseline outputs (results/*.csv) with a regression test so you notice if they drift.

verification.reason: The mechanism is correct. One rng is created per model (e2_dispatch.py:52) and consumed sequentially by stochastic and then cvar each day (policies.py:120-121), so there are no common random numbers and inserting a policy before them shifts later draws. The impact is Monte Carlo noise on a 40-scenario SAA averaged over 200 days, not a systematic bias. Baselines can also be preserved simply by appending new policies after the existing ones.
